module

public import FormalConjecturesUtil

/-!
# Erdős Problem 931

*Reference:* [erdosproblems.com/931](https://www.erdosproblems.com/931)
-/

@[expose] public section

namespace Erdos931

/--
Let $k_1 \geq k_2 \geq 3$. Are there only finitely many $n_2\geq n_1 + k_1$
such that
$$
  \prod_{1\leq i\leq k_1}(n_1 + i)\ \text{and}\ \prod_{1\leq j\leq k_2} (n_2 + j)
$$
have the same prime factors?
-/
@[category research open, AMS 11]
theorem erdos_931 : answer(sorry) ↔ ∀ᵉ (k₁ : ℕ) (k₂ ≥ 3), k₂ ≤ k₁ →
    { (n₁, n₂) | n₁ + k₁ ≤ n₂ ∧
      (∏ i ∈ Finset.Icc 1 k₁, (n₁ + i)).primeFactors =
      (∏ j ∈ Finset.Icc 1 k₂, (n₂ + j)).primeFactors }.Finite := by
  sorry

/--
Erdős thought perhaps if the two products have the same factors then
$n_2 > 2(n_1 + k_1)$.
It is an open question whether this is true when allowing a finite number of counterexamples.
-/
@[category research open, AMS 11]
theorem erdos_931.variants.additional_condition : answer(sorry) ↔ ∀ᵉ (k₁ : ℕ) (k₂ ≥ 3), k₂ ≤ k₁ →
    {(n₁, n₂) | n₁ + k₁ ≤ n₂ ∧ n₂ ≤ 2 * (n₁ + k₁) ∧
      (∏ i ∈ Finset.Icc 1 k₁, (n₁ + i)).primeFactors =
      (∏ j ∈ Finset.Icc 1 k₂, (n₂ + j)).primeFactors}.Finite := by
  sorry

/--
In fact there exist counterexamples, like this one found by AlphaProof.
-/
@[category research solved, AMS 11]
theorem erdos_931.variants.additional_condition_nonempty : ∃ (k₁ k₂ : ℕ), ∃ (_h₁ : k₂ ≤ k₁), ∃ (_h₂ : 3 ≤ k₂),
  {(n₁, n₂) | n₁ + k₁ ≤ n₂ ∧ n₂ ≤ 2 * (n₁ + k₁) ∧
      (∏ i ∈ Finset.Icc 1 k₁, (n₁ + i)).primeFactors =
      (∏ j ∈ Finset.Icc 1 k₂, (n₂ + j)).primeFactors}.Nonempty := by
  use 10, 3, (by norm_num), (by norm_num)
  use (0, 13)
  norm_num [Finset.prod_Icc_succ_top]
  norm_num +decide [Nat.primeFactors, Nat.primeFactorsList]

/--
Erdős was unable to prove that if the two products have the same factors
then there must exist a prime between $n_1$ and $n_2$.
-/
@[category research open, AMS 11]
theorem erdos_931.variants.exists_prime (k₁ k₂ n₁ n₂ : ℕ) (h₁ : k₂ ≤ k₁) (h₂ : 3 ≤ k₂)
    (h₃ : n₁ + k₁ ≤ n₂) (h₄ : (∏ i ∈ Finset.Icc 1 k₁, (n₁ + i)).primeFactors =
      (∏ j ∈ Finset.Icc 1 k₂, (n₂ + j)).primeFactors) :
    ∃ (p : ℕ), p.Prime ∧ n₁ ≤ p ∧ p ≤ n₂ := by
  sorry

end Erdos931

reformulations.difference: The original paper describes nonexistence of equal prime supports when n₁ and n₂ lie between the same two consecutive primes. Lean instead concludes that equal prime supports imply a prime in the closed interval [n₁,n₂].
reformulations.equivalence_argument: For a ≤ b with b ≥ 2, absence of a prime in [a,b] is equivalent to the existence of consecutive primes p < q with p < a ≤ b < q. In one direction the gap contains no prime; in the other, choose the greatest prime below a and the least prime at least a. The file's hypotheses imply n₁ ≤ n₂ and n₂ ≥ 3, so this equivalence applies, and contraposition gives the Lean conclusion. Thus inclusion of the endpoints is justified by the original prime-gap wording. The interval/gap equivalence was proved without using any sorry theorem in /workspace/review/gap-equivalence.lean.

could_not_verify: Erdos931.erdos_931: Could not fully certify the parameter scope against the cited webpage. The original paper expresses the length restriction using min(k₁,k₂), without explicitly imposing k₂ ≤ k₁, whereas Lean fixes ordered lengths before asserting finiteness. Without the webpage's precise formulation, I cannot classify that difference as a defect or an intended specialization.

Erdos931.erdos_931.variants.additional_condition: The original paper poses the inequality without exceptions. I verified that Lean correctly expresses finitely many violations for each fixed pair of lengths, but could not independently confirm the modern finite-exception variant's intended scope or current status on the inaccessible webpage.

Erdos931.erdos_931.variants.exists_prime: The conclusion is the verified prime-gap reformulation recorded above, but full source-scope verification still depends on confirming the ordered-length restriction k₂ ≤ k₁ on the cited webpage. Its current open/solved status could not be checked there.
review.notes: No confirmed defect, but the source comparison is incomplete: https://www.erdosproblems.com/931 remained behind a Cloudflare challenge, including in a browser. I read the original paper instead; the independent status table still records the main problem as open. Lean experiments verified product positivity for all natural starting points and lengths, equality of primeFactors as equality of prime-divisor supports, the quantifier expansions, finiteness of pairs versus their second-coordinate projection, and the finite-exception encoding. The displayed counterexample evaluates to products 3628800 and 3360 with common prime support {2,3,5,7}; its existing proof has no sorryAx dependency. All final proof-check files compiled successfully under /workspace/review/.
